subject: Space
heading: You are seeing the sun as it was eight minutes ago
body: Light takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross 150 million km. If it went out you would carry on reading in bright daylight for the length of a song.

subject: Space
heading: There is a planet where it rains glass, sideways
body: HD 189733b is cobalt blue and its winds run at 5,400 mph. The blue is silicate particles — glass — blown horizontally through the atmosphere.

subject: Space
heading: Saturn would float
body: It is less dense than water. Find an ocean big enough and the whole planet would sit on top of it.

subject: Space
heading: A day on Venus is longer than its year
body: It turns once every 243 Earth days and orbits in 225. The sun rises in the west, twice a year, very slowly.

subject: Animals
heading: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
body: Two pump to the gills, one to the body — and that one stops when they swim, which is why they prefer crawling.

subject: Animals
heading: A shrimp can boil water by clicking
body: The pistol shrimp snaps its claw fast enough to form a collapsing bubble that reaches thousands of degrees for a fraction of a millisecond.

subject: Animals
heading: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings
body: The last stretch of intestine has patches of differing elasticity that mould them. Cubes do not roll away, which matters if you mark territory with them.

subject: Animals
heading: One jellyfish can reverse its own ageing
body: Turritopsis dohrnii reverts to its juvenile stage under stress and starts again. In principle it need never die of old age.

subject: Animals
heading: Crows hold grudges, and tell their friends
body: They recognise individual human faces, remember who treated them badly, and pass the grievance to birds that were never there.

subject: Everyday
heading: Honey never goes off
body: Jars from Egyptian tombs are still edible. Too acidic and too dry for bacteria, and bees add an enzyme that makes hydrogen peroxide.

subject: Everyday
heading: Bananas are clones
body: Almost every banana sold is a Cavendish, grown from cuttings — genetically one plant. That is why a single fungus can threaten the entire crop, and did once before.

subject: Everyday
heading: Carrots were purple first
body: Orange ones were bred in the Netherlands in the 16th century. The colour you think of as natural is a few hundred years old.

subject: Everyday
heading: The QWERTY layout is not slowing you down
body: The jamming story outlived the typewriter. Tests against faster layouts find differences small enough to vanish with practice.

subject: Everyday
heading: Bubble wrap was invented as wallpaper
body: It failed. Then it was sold as greenhouse insulation. It failed again. Only on the third attempt did anyone think of packaging.

subject: History
heading: Zero was banned in Florence
body: India had a symbol for it by the 7th century; Europe resisted 400 years, and Florence outlawed it in 1299. A digit meaning nothing looked like a way to forge a ledger.

subject: History
heading: Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire
body: Teaching at Oxford began around 1096. Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325. Two things that feel like different eras overlapped by centuries.

subject: History
heading: Cleopatra lived closer to the moon landing than to the pyramids
body: The Great Pyramid was already 2,500 years old when she was born. She is 2,000 years from us.

subject: History
heading: The last execution by guillotine was in 1977
body: The same year Star Wars opened and the Apple II went on sale. France kept it until 1981.

subject: Language
heading: Every word for "brother" sounds the same
body: Bhrātṛ in Sanskrit, frater in Latin, bróðir in Norse. They did not borrow it — they inherited it from one language nobody wrote down, spoken 6,000 years ago.

subject: Language
heading: Quarantine is a length of time
body: Quaranta giorni — forty days. Venice held arriving ships that long during the plague, and the word carries the number inside it.

subject: Language
heading: "Nice" used to mean stupid
body: From Latin nescius, not-knowing. It drifted through foolish, fussy, precise, and only landed on pleasant in the 1700s.

subject: Body
heading: You replace your skeleton about every ten years
body: Osteoclasts dissolve old bone; osteoblasts lay down new. The shape stays, the material does not. You are the same skeleton the way a river is the same river.

subject: Body
heading: Your gut has more bacteria than you have cells
body: Roughly 38 trillion of them to 30 trillion of you. By headcount you are a minority in your own body.

subject: Body
heading: Nothing you touch is actually touching you
body: The floor holds you up by electromagnetic repulsion between electrons. What you feel as contact is a force at a distance.

subject: Earth
heading: Africa is bigger than every map has shown you
body: The USA, China, India and most of Europe fit inside it at once. Mercator stretches the poles to keep angles true and squashes the equator to pay for it.

subject: Earth
heading: The sky is blue for the reason sunsets are red
body: Air scatters short wavelengths hardest. At sunset the light crosses far more air, the blue is scattered away entirely, and what is left is what reaches you.

subject: Earth
heading: Ice floats, and almost nothing else does
body: Water expands when it freezes because the hydrogen bonds lock into a lattice with gaps. If it did not, lakes would freeze from the bottom and stay frozen.

subject: Earth
heading: Russia spans eleven time zones
body: When it is Monday morning in Kaliningrad it is Monday evening in Kamchatka. One country, one working day, twelve hours apart.

subject: Making
heading: Blue was the most expensive colour for 600 years
body: Ultramarine came from lapis lazuli, mined in one valley in Afghanistan. It cost more than gold, which is why painters saved it for the Virgin Mary robes.

subject: Making
heading: An octave is a doubling
body: The A above middle C is 440 vibrations a second; the next A is 880. Every octave doubles, and that ratio is why they sound like the same note.

subject: Making
heading: The Eiffel Tower is taller in summer
body: Iron expands. It grows about 15cm on a hot day and leans slightly away from the sun.

subject: Study
heading: Reading it twice is one of the weakest ways to learn
body: Recall beats review: shut the book, write what you remember, then check. It feels worse and works better, which is exactly why people avoid it.

subject: Study
heading: Sleep is when the learning gets filed
body: The hippocampus replays the day during deep sleep and hands it to the cortex. Revising until 2am and sitting the paper at 9 skips the step that makes it stick.

subject: Study
heading: Spacing beats cramming at equal total time
body: Six hours over six days beats six hours in one. Each time you nearly forget and then retrieve it, the memory is rebuilt stronger.

subject: Money
heading: The £ sign is a letter L
body: Libra — Roman for pound weight. The two strokes through it mean abbreviation. Same root as lb for pounds, which is why neither looks like the word it stands for.

subject: Money
heading: A Post Office was once the biggest bank in the country
body: Before high street banking reached most towns, the Post Office Savings Bank held more accounts than every bank combined. It is why post offices still feel institutional.

subject: Money
heading: Nobody agrees what a billion is
body: It meant a million million in Britain until the 1970s and a thousand million in America. The government switched officially in 1974 and old textbooks did not.

subject: Sport
heading: The marathon distance comes from a royal box
body: It was 25 miles until London 1908, when the start moved to Windsor Castle so the children could watch from the nursery. The extra 385 yards has been standard ever since.

subject: Sport
heading: Football nearly had no crossbar
body: Until 1875 the goal was two posts and a tape. Teams argued endlessly about whether a ball had passed over or under it, which is a fair description of most sport before rules.

subject: Sport
heading: Table tennis was banned in the Soviet Union for 20 years
body: Officials decided it was harmful to the eyes. The ban lasted from 1930 to 1950, by which time the rest of the world had a considerable head start.

subject: Tech
heading: The first computer bug was a moth
body: Grace Hopper taped it into the Harvard Mark II logbook in 1947 with the note "first actual case of bug being found". The word already meant a fault; she found a literal one.

subject: Tech
heading: Wi-Fi does not stand for anything
body: A branding agency invented it to sound like hi-fi. IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence is what it replaced, and the meaninglessness was the point.

subject: Tech
heading: The @ sign was nearly extinct
body: It survived on typewriter keyboards as an accounting shorthand — 3 widgets @ £2. Ray Tomlinson picked it for email in 1971 because nobody used it in names.

subject: Tech
heading: Nokia started as a paper mill
body: Then rubber boots, then cables, then phones. Companies that last a century rarely do it by staying in the same business.

subject: Nature
heading: Trees talk through fungus
body: Mycorrhizal networks link roots across a forest, moving sugar and warning signals between trees. A dying tree will push its carbon into its neighbours.

subject: Nature
heading: A single aspen colony can be one organism
body: Pando in Utah is 47,000 trunks sharing one root system, thought to weigh 6,000 tonnes. It is possibly the heaviest living thing on Earth.

subject: Nature
heading: Bamboo can grow nearly a metre a day
body: Some species add 90cm in 24 hours — fast enough that you could watch it if you were patient. It is a grass, not a tree.

subject: Nature
heading: Lightning is five times hotter than the sun
body: About 30,000°C at the channel, against 5,500°C at the sun surface. Only for a few millionths of a second, which is the only reason anyone survives being near it.

subject: Buildings
heading: The Empire State Building went up in 410 days
body: Finished ahead of schedule and under budget in 1931. Modern equivalents take four or five years, and mostly for reasons that have nothing to do with the building.

subject: Buildings
heading: Notre-Dame took nearly 200 years
body: Begun 1163, largely finished 1345. Nobody who laid the first stone saw the roof. Cathedrals were built by people who accepted they would not see the end.

subject: Buildings
heading: Venice is built on wooden piles that never rotted
body: Millions of alder trunks driven into the mud. Without oxygen the wood petrified instead of decaying, and it has held the city up for 1,200 years.

subject: People
heading: The inventor of the Pringles tube is buried in one
body: Fredric Baur was so pleased with it that he asked to be interred in one. His children stopped at a supermarket on the way to the funeral to buy the tube.

subject: People
heading: Nikola Tesla died owing money in a New York hotel
body: He had 300 patents and had lit the world, and spent his last years feeding pigeons. Being right and being paid are different achievements.

subject: People
heading: Roald Dahl helped invent a brain valve
body: After his son was injured, he worked with an engineer and a surgeon on the Wade-Dahl-Till valve for hydrocephalus. It was used on thousands of children.

subject: Oddities
heading: There is a town where it is illegal to die
body: Longyearbyen in Svalbard. The permafrost stops bodies decomposing, so burials preserve whatever killed you — including the 1918 flu, still viable in graves there.

subject: Oddities
heading: A cloud weighs about 500 tonnes
body: An average cumulus holds roughly that much water. It stays up because the droplets are tiny and the air beneath is warmer and rising.

subject: Oddities
heading: The shortest war lasted 38 minutes
body: Britain against Zanzibar, 1896. The Sultan surrendered before the ships had finished firing, and the war was over before most people knew it had begun.

subject: Oddities
heading: Scotland has 421 words for snow
body: Feefle, flindrikin, snitter, spitters, unbrak. A language grows vocabulary where its speakers need precision, which is why English has so many words for rain.
